title: What is known about 1RB0LC_1RC0RC_1LD0RB_1LA0LE_1LD1LF_1LD---
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB0LC_1RC0RC_1LD0RB_1LA0LE_1LD1LF_1LD---.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: Open. The tape is a list of segments, each with a two-state marker that toggles like a binary counter digit while shifting one pair of cells at a time; segment sizes run near powers of two (511, 1023, 2047, …). The left end grows only 69 cells in 109 steps.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (F1); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 90,039 cells have been visited and 45,013 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: Growth shape: power/sqrt
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like a power of the step count other than 1/2 (fitted exponent 0.17). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.527).

claims.title: The structure of the run
claims.text: Bouncer whose tape is a list of segments (10)^x M (10)^y 1, with a marker M = 0 or 000: the sweeps toggle the markers like the digits of a binary counter, each toggle moving material between the two halves of a segment.

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known. No closed rule set has been found; see the README for what a proof would need.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows. This page runs the machine in your browser and describes the structure seen in its run.

facts.text: No halt in the C simulator; 90,039 cells visited.
No halt, proved in Lean; the first 10,000 by the kernel alone.
binary-counter-like bouncer with sliding digit markers (chaotic)

sections.heading: What the tape looks like
html: The tape is a list of segments (10)x M (10)y 1 where the marker M is 0 or 000. On each sweep the rightmost segments toggle their markers like the low digits of a binary counter; a toggle moves the marker one pair to the right (x+1, y−1) or flips its form. The right end grows 2 pairs per sweep; segment sizes cluster near 2k−1. When a segment's y is used up the segment structure changes, which is where the run becomes irregular.

sections.heading: Where it could halt
html: The only halting transition is F reading 1. A closed tape language with windows of 6 cells (bbtools.ctl) covers the run but still allows halts, with only a local constraint near the head: the head cell and the cells to its right read 110101 or 110110 (a 1 under the head, then 1, 0, 1 ...). Nothing confines a halt to an edge.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like a power of the step count other than 1/2 (fitted exponent 0.17). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.527).
After 109 steps the tape spans 90,039 cells (57 left of the start, 59,726 right), with a density of 1s of 0.5.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

summary: Bouncer whose tape is a list of segments (10)^x M (10)^y 1, with a marker M = 0 or 000: the sweeps toggle the markers like the digits of a binary counter, each toggle moving material between the two halves of a segment.
family: binary-counter-like bouncer with sliding digit markers (chaotic)
